CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support the long-term effectiveness of exposure-based CBT for anxiety disorders, with most patients remaining stable without further treatment. Clinicians can reassure patients about sustained benefits but should monitor those with residual symptoms, as they may require additional support. Further research is needed to optimize outcomes for non-remitters.

item.title: [10] Analysis of the placebo response model and its influencing factors in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a model-based meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study used a model-based meta-analysis (MBMA) of 79 placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials (RCTs) to quantify the longitudinal trajectory of the placebo response in ADHD, identify trial- and patient-level predictors, and compare pediatric vs. adult populations to inform future trial design.
FINDINGS: Placebo responses on ADHD-RS and CGI-S followed non-linear trajectories, plateauing at ~6 weeks (ADHD-RS) and ~10 weeks (CGI-S). Larger sample sizes, recent trials, multicenter designs, industry sponsorship, and use of stimulant comparators were associated with higher placebo responses. Pediatric and adult placebo trajectories were similar in shape and magnitude.
INTERPRETATION: The MBMA leverages a large dataset and advanced modeling, strengthening internal validity for describing placebo dynamics. However, as an aggregate analysis, it cannot infer causality for predictors and may be confounded by unmeasured trial-level factors. The similarity in pediatric/adult placebo trajectories is robust but does not address potential differences in active treatment effects. The clinical significance is primarily for trial methodology rather than patient care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings can guide sample size calculations and endpoint selection in future ADHD trials but do not alter current clinical practice regarding placebo response management.

item.title: [9] The Impact of Psychological Therapies on Well-Being and Quality of Life in Adult Chronic Migraine Patients: A Systematic Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month, ≥8 migraine days) severely impairs quality of life and is often complicated by insomnia and emotional distress. This systematic review examined whether psychological therapies (mindfulness, CBT for insomnia) improve well-being and quality of life in adults with chronic migraine.
FINDINGS: Four heterogeneous studies were included (mindfulness-based interventions and CBTi). Mindfulness reduced headache frequency and disability, improved pain acceptance and mood, and showed sustained benefits up to 12 months post-intervention; combining mindfulness with tDCS suggested additive effects. CBTi improved sleep quality and led to delayed but meaningful reductions in headache days. Emotional outcomes (depression) improved modestly; anxiety outcomes were inconsistent.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is very small (only four studies) and heterogeneous in interventions and outcomes, precluding meta-analysis. Methodological limitations include lack of blinding, small samples, and variability in comparators and follow-up durations. While results suggest psychological therapies may improve several domains of functioning, the strength of evidence is low and prone to bias. Larger, well-controlled RCTs with standardized outcomes are needed to confirm efficacy and identify which patients benefit most.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify changing first-line migraine treatments but suggest psychological therapies—particularly mindfulness and CBTi—could be considered as adjuncts in multidisciplinary care for motivated patients with chronic migraine and comorbid insomnia or mood symptoms.

item.title: [7] Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for bipolar disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The chapter reviews neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) for bipolar disorder, integrating neural mechanisms (prefrontal-limbic dysfunction, reward processing, circadian disruption) into psychoeducational content. It aims to bridge neuroscience with clinical practice but lacks empirical evaluation of NIPE’s efficacy in bipolar disorder.
FINDINGS: The review outlines NIPE’s theoretical framework, translating neural mechanisms into psychoeducational strategies (e.g., cognitive monitoring, circadian interventions). It proposes mechanisms for improved outcomes (e.g., adherence, self-efficacy) but notes no randomized trials or robust empirical data exist to confirm these benefits.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is purely theoretical, with no direct clinical data. Strengths include a plausible mechanistic rationale and practical delivery considerations (e.g., state-dependent insight). However, the lack of empirical validation, potential biases (e.g., narrative review), and untested assumptions limit confidence. The proposed effect sizes and clinical relevance remain speculative.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: NIPE may offer a promising adjunct to bipolar psychoeducation, but its use should be considered experimental. Clinicians should await randomized trials before adopting NIPE, as current recommendations are based on mechanistic plausibility rather than proven efficacy.

item.title: [6] Risk of falls and delirium associated with dual orexin receptor antagonists versus benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults with dementia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study compared safety outcomes (falls, delirium, hospitalisation, mortality, and emergency department visits) between dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs) and benzodiazepines (BZDs)/Z-drugs in older adults (≥65 years) with dementia and insomnia, using retrospective electronic health record data. The clinical question is whether DORAs are safer alternatives to BZDs/Z-drugs in this high-risk population.
FINDINGS: In 734 propensity score-matched pairs (mean age 83.5 years; 65–66% female), DORA use was associated with significantly lower risks over 12 months: falls (HR 0.35, 95% CI 0.18–0.71; P = 0.003), delirium (HR 0.39, 95% CI 0.23–0.65; P < 0.001), hospitalisation (HR 0.31, 95% CI 0.21–0.47; P < 0.001), and emergency department visits (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.20–0.50; P < 0.001). Mortality showed no significant difference (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.53–1.11; P = 0.154).
INTERPRETATION: This retrospective cohort study provides moderate-strength evidence suggesting DORAs may reduce falls, delirium, and healthcare utilisation compared with BZDs/Z-drugs in older adults with dementia. However, residual confounding is likely due to the observational design (e.g., unmeasured illness severity, prescribing bias). The large effect sizes (HRs ~0.3–0.4) are clinically meaningful but should be interpreted cautiously. Confirmation via prospective randomised trials is needed before practice changes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: DORAs may represent a safer option than BZDs/Z-drugs for insomnia in older adults with dementia, potentially reducing falls and delirium. Clinicians should consider this evidence when weighing risks/benefits but await stronger evidence before definitive practice changes.

item.title: [6] Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for depression: From stress to adaptive brain recovery.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review explores whether neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE)—which integrates contemporary affective neuroscience, stress biology, neuroplasticity, and brain-circuit research into patient education—can improve outcomes for adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) by enhancing understanding, self-management, and engagement with treatment.
FINDINGS: The paper synthesizes evidence on conventional psychoeducation in mood disorders and argues that NIPE may reduce self-blame and stigma, strengthen agency, and support sustained recovery by framing depression as a disorder of adaptive brain recovery. No quantitative outcomes (e.g., effect sizes, p-values) are reported, as this is a narrative review rather than a trial or meta-analysis.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, the evidence is conceptual and lacks direct empirical data. Strengths include integration of recent neuroscience and clinical rationale; limitations include absence of systematic evidence synthesis, no quantitative estimates, and potential selection bias in cited studies. The clinical significance of NIPE remains unproven pending controlled trials.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: NIPE may offer a theoretically sound adjunct to standard psychoeducation, but current evidence does not justify changing practice. Clinicians may consider it as a communication tool while awaiting empirical validation.

item.title: [6] Concomitant Psychotropic Medication Is Associated with Reduced Outcomes of Trauma-Focused Psychotherapy for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether concomitant psychotropic medication at the start of trauma-focused psychotherapy for PTSD reduces treatment efficacy in a real-world cohort. Using target-trial emulation with double machine learning and inverse probability weighting, it assessed changes in CAPS-5 scores from pre- to post-treatment in 6,125 adults receiving standardized trauma-focused therapy at a Dutch center (2021–2024).
FINDINGS: Mean CAPS-5 scores improved by 25.7 points overall (Cohen’s d = −2.30). Psychotropic co-medication (n = 1,382) was associated with a 2.52-point smaller improvement (−9.4%, 95% CI −10.0 to −8.9; d = −1.11, E = 10.0) versus no co-medication. The negative association persisted at 6-month follow-up (d = −0.42). Antidepressants (d = −0.28; follow-up d = −0.56), amitriptyline, mirtazapine, anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, fluoxetine, zolpidem, and zopiclone showed consistent associations with poorer outcomes across sensitivity analyses.
INTERPRETATION: The study used robust target-trial emulation and sensitivity analyses to mitigate confounding, suggesting a modest but consistent reduction in psychotherapy efficacy with certain psychotropic co-medications. However, the observational design precludes causal inference, and effect sizes, while statistically significant, may not translate into clinically dramatic differences. Unmeasured confounding and selection bias remain possible despite E-value robustness.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest clinicians may consider tapering or substituting specific psychotropic medications—particularly certain antidepressants and sedatives—before initiating trauma-focused psychotherapy to optimize outcomes. Routine practice should balance this potential benefit against risks of medication discontinuation and relapse. Further randomized trials are needed to confirm causality and guide tapering strategies.

item.title: [15] Beyond scales: Artificial intelligence, language, and behavior in suicide risk modeling-a narrative review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether artificial intelligence (AI) methods—machine learning, deep learning, and large language models—can improve the identification of individuals at imminent suicide risk by integrating diverse data sources (EHRs, clinical notes, speech, neuroimaging, passive sensing). It focuses on clinically relevant performance metrics, validation practices, and implementation challenges in routine psychiatric care.
FINDINGS: The review synthesizes evidence across multiple data modalities (structured records, natural language processing, speech/behavioral signals, neuroimaging, and passive sensing) to assess AI’s potential in predicting suicidal thoughts and behaviors. It highlights the need for robust discrimination and calibration metrics, temporal and external validation, and interpretable outputs for clinical decision-making. Key barriers include class imbalance, label noise, dataset shift, limited prospective evaluation, and ethical concerns such as privacy, bias, and governance.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study does not provide quantitative effect sizes or head-to-head comparisons but instead maps the landscape of AI applications in suicide risk prediction. The strength of the evidence lies in its comprehensive overview of modalities and methodological challenges, while its weakness is the lack of systematic quality assessment or pooled estimates. The clinical relevance of AI tools remains uncertain until prospective, externally validated studies demonstrate improved patient outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current AI models are not yet ready for routine use in suicide risk stratification; clinicians should remain cautious about adopting unvalidated tools. Future priorities include multimodal longitudinal cohorts and pragmatic trials to assess whether AI decision support improves prevention outcomes and care pathways.
